A1.notes.Q3: Course grades and credits are already used, so a small jump is okay to catch early signs before they drop out completely.
A1.notes.Q4: Students hate being told they 'don't belong' or that a black box algorithm flagged them as risky.
A1.notes.Q5: We need to support all students equally; missing an international student because of bias is unacceptable discrimination.
A1.notes.Q6: If the system flags someone, they need help NOW, not once a year.
A1.notes.Q7: With personalized emails calling out their situation, false positives feel like harassment and damage trust severely.

A2.notes.Q3: Grades matter for fairness (moderate gain okay). Absalon data is intrusive (late submissions, page views) and often proxies behavior we already know about via emails; I'd avoid it.
A2.notes.Q4: Students need to know why they were flagged to trust the system and actually use help. Black boxes undermine our role as advisors.
A2.notes.Q5: Overall hit rate must drop slightly (about 3 students) but only if it ensures we don't falsely flag vulnerable groups, prioritizing false negatives over false positives.
A2.notes.Q6: Immediate outreach is crucial; waiting risks students disengaging entirely. But 'continuous' means the moment they cross a threshold, not an annual check.
A2.notes.Q7: Personalized messages are better than generic ones, so I'd accept more false positives to reach those who truly need it sooner rather than later.

A3.notes.Q3: Course performance is fine as academic tracking. High-school GPA feels like a past-life judgment I can't influence, so I won't use that online tool for me or my advisees.
A3.notes.Q4: If the rule is simple, we can discuss it directly in our meetings with students. 'Why are you flagged?' needs to be answerable by a human quickly; complex models cause anxiety.
A3.notes.Q5: It's unacceptable if the model misses marginalized groups entirely because they get left behind. A small drop in overall catch rate is necessary to fix this bias.
A3.notes.Q6: Early detection saves credits and stress. Students need constant nudges, not once a year when it's too late to recover.
A3.notes.Q7: With generic emails, we cast a wide net as they're low impact. With personalized advice from advisors, precision matters more than volume; don't overwhelm anyone.
A3.Q8.1: I worry that 'academic difficulty' definitions are too narrow and miss students struggling with existential issues or mental health problems who haven't yet failed courses.

S1.notes.Q3: I've dropped out before, so grades matter (large threshold). School background seems relevant for me as a first-gen student (moderate), but I don't want my age or race flagged.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I'm being contacted, especially if it's sensitive info like disability status. Complex black-box models make me anxious.
S1.notes.Q5: Missing students in groups that already face barriers hurts us more than accidentally flagging one person who is fine. Fairness can't cost too much though (only 3%).
S1.notes.Q6: A generic email feels safer and less intrusive than a personal call, but I might miss out on specialized help if it's not personalized.
S1.notes.Q7: If the outreach is an actual advisor meeting tailored to me (like my disability history), I don't want false positives causing unnecessary stress. Being contacted only if truly needed feels right.

S2.notes.Q3: Grades are useful (large threshold needed due to part-time stress). High school data feels invasive for a non-EU student but fair is okay if it boosts equality.
S2.notes.Q4: Black box models terrify me when I might be flagged unfairly by a hidden variable I can't fix.
S2.notes.Q5: We don't need to save everyone; we must ensure the system doesn't wrongly flag vulnerable groups (false positives) over working ones.
S2.notes.Q6: One email isn't enough if I'm struggling mid-semester; immediate outreach is crucial.
S2.notes.Q7: Generic emails annoy me as a worker/student, but personalized ones are helpful only if accurate.

S3.notes.Q3: Credits and grades are essential because they reflect my reduced load due to health, not discrimination. Disability data is critical for fairness but must be protected strictly; I'd accept small improvement thresholds if it targets me specifically.
S3.notes.Q4: As someone with a health condition, I need clear reasons to understand why support is offered. Black-box models feel intrusive and untrustworthy compared to the simple credit rule we already use.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness matters, but missing my need for support due to illness is unacceptable. The model should prioritize catching students I might miss rather than ensuring perfect accuracy across all groups.
S3.notes.Q6: I don't know when my health might deteriorate again; continuous monitoring via personalized outreach gives me the chance to be supported early before I crash.
S3.notes.Q7: A generic email is too vague for someone with a disability who needs tailored help, but sending it to everyone creates noise. A balance seems most respectful of privacy and need.
S3.Q8.1: I worry about the long-term data collection habits this creates; students might feel they can only succeed if their every move is tracked digitally.

S4.notes.Q3: I trust course data (grades/credits) but not behavioral tracking like Absalon views as it feels intrusive without a huge gain in identifying me or peers.
S4.notes.Q4: Very low explainability breaks trust completely with me and advisors; I need to know the specific reasons why.
S4.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial for avoiding bias, but being fair across groups often means missing more people overall which feels counterproductive for support systems.
S4.notes.Q6: I prefer a personal meeting because I don't want automated outreach; frequency matters less than the quality and empathy of the interaction.
S4.notes.Q7: General emails are too impersonal, so even if they miss me once or twice, I'd rather avoid unnecessary contact than deal with spammy messages.

S5.notes.Q3: I'm from outside the EU, so I worry about my data being used beyond Denmark's context without consent. Tracking late submissions in Absalon feels like constant surveillance; only large improvements would justify it for me personally.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I'm flagged so an advisor can help me specifically, not just vaguely. A 'black box' prediction makes the outreach feel threatening rather than supportive.
S5.notes.Q5: As a female international student in STEM, I worry models might systematically overlook me compared to Danish male peers unless we prioritize catching everyone over total numbers.
S5.notes.Q6: Early is better than late for me right now; I don't want to wait until the end of a semester before getting support.
S5.notes.Q7: With personalized emails, false positives are really intrusive since they feel targeted at me personally; I'd rather miss some cases than have advisors waste time on students who don't need help.

S6.notes.Q3: Course grades matter, but online browsing data feels like surveillance given my previous dropout from a local uni.
S6.notes.Q4: I can't trust a system that guesses my struggles without showing me exactly why I'm being flagged.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness means ensuring the support actually reaches people like me who get overlooked because of language or background issues.
S6.notes.Q6: A generic email might be ignored; a personalized message shows I'm being seen, which is important given my past failure.
S6.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach should only happen for high-risk cases to avoid alienating students who are trying their best.
S6.Q8.1: I worry that focusing so much on prediction might make the university ignore context-specific problems that aren't easily digitizable or measured by Absalon data.

S7.notes.Q3: Course grades are fine for tracking progress, but online activity (Absalon data) feels like surveillance since I already know my study habits struggle due to dyslexia using extra time. Sensitive personal data triggers high privacy concerns unless we can prove massive benefit.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I am flagged so the advisor can help me understand my struggle, not just let an algorithm decide without explanation.
S7.notes.Q5: Missing support is bad for everyone regardless of nationality or background, but if I'm already marginalized by bias, fairness means catching me specifically so the system doesn't overlook my disability barriers.
S7.notes.Q6: Since I have a condition affecting my studies, early intervention is crucial to prevent me from falling behind again like previous attempts.
S7.notes.Q7: For general info, it's okay if some don't need support (better awareness). But for personalized advice based on sensitive data, minimizing false positives is vital to avoid stigmatization.
S7.Q8.1: Students often lack context about the specific barriers they face due to neurodivergence; models might misinterpret extra time requests as 'difficulty' without understanding it's a support strategy.

S8.notes.Q3: Using past high school grades feels risky for privacy, maybe only acceptable if it really helps me find support I'd miss.
S8.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I was flagged, especially after dropping out once before. Without it, the email feels like punishment.
S8.notes.Q5: If a model misses me or other vulnerable students because of bias, that's worse than missing some others. I can't afford to be misidentified as struggling.
S8.notes.Q6: I might not notice until I'm too far behind, so constant checks are necessary for people like me who struggle.
S8.notes.Q7: Personalized messages feel stigmatizing if sent to many. Too broad emails get ignored; too few might miss critical cases without warning.

S9.notes.Q3: I'm hesitant about Absalon data (Q3.4) because I've already had my digital footprint analyzed for grading; that feels intrusive enough on its own without behavioral tracking. However, grades are essential context since I have a difficult pace.
S9.notes.Q4: High explainability is non-negotiable for me; I need to understand why I'm flagged, especially given my health struggles so it's not just an automated error.
S9.notes.Q5: As a first-gen student with international background, I'd trade general effectiveness for fairness if it specifically helped my group (nationality/first-gen) be identified as reliably.
S9.notes.Q6: Generic emails are too vague when you have complex issues like mental health; I need a human connection, even if it's less frequent.
S9.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach is high-stakes but low volume per student means missing cases costs more than the false positives from slightly fewer contacts.
